newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein's Adams presses for dialogue with Britain.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein's Adams presses for dialogue with Britain.

text.p: Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams urged Britain on Monday to sanction talks with his party to try to restore a ceasefire his IRA guerrilla allies broke one year ago, plunging Northern Ireland back into violence.
Adams, speaking against a background of weekly IRA attacks, said the situation in the province was deteriorating rapidly and urged action before the British election due by May 22.

He called on British Prime Minister John Major to allow government officials to meet representatives of his party to discuss a proposal for a new Irish Republican Army (IRA) truce in its war against British rule of the province.
Major rejected proposals which Adams and Irish nationalist peace broker John Hume drew up last October in an attempt to get Sinn Fein a seat at peace talks under way in Belfast.
"Let him (Major) now take the time to again look over the propositions which he rejected in December,"Adams said in a statement issued in Belfast.

"If he isn't happy with what John Hume and I proposed, let him authorise some of his officials to meet with Sinn Fein officials and endeavour to work out the minutiae of what is required," the statement said.
Sources close to Hume and Adams say that the IRA is willing to declare a new truce providing it wins Sinn Fein immediate and unconditional entry to the Belfast negotiations.
But the IRA also wants pledges that its goal of a united Ireland will be on the agenda and that a broad time-frame for the talks will be fixed to ensure there is a conclusion.

Adams' party is barred from the negotiations because of IRA violence. They group Hume's Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) and Protestant Unionist parties which oppose talks with Sinn Fein and want the province to stay British.

Major last year toughened London's conditions for Sinn Fein's inclusion in the talks by stating that any new IRA truce would have to be permanent and subject to a review period before Sinn Fein could join the negotiations.

Britain has refused all direct contact with Sinn Fein since its IRA allies ended a 17-month truce on February 19 last year and returned to its campaign against British rule by attacking targets in London, Germany and Northern Ireland itself.

Adams' statement was seen as a further attempt by Sinn Fein and Hume to get Northern Ireland back near the top of Britain's political agenda before Major fights a rearguard action against the Labour opposition at the forthcoming election.
Sinn Fein and the SDLP fear that if Labour leader Tony Blair wins the election Northern Ireland will slide down his agenda as he strives to overhaul the legacy of years of Conservative rule.
Northern Ireland has teetered on the brink of total sectarian warfare since the IRA bombed Britain's Northern Ireland army base last October 7, killing one soldier.

It marked the first strike by the IRA in Northern Ireland itself since the guerrillas' August 31, 1994 ceasefire and put at risk a matching truce by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas fighting to maintain British rule.
The IRA has bombed British security targets every few days this year but has failed in what police say is a deliberate attempt to kill a security force target to provoke Loyalist retaliation.
Police believe the IRA is determined to provoke such revenge attacks to present the next British government with a dangerous security problem which will require urgent political action.
